- Core translation of Benzon's method into CS/ML terms
  - Sidenote's "Benzon's term \u2192 CS/ML interpretation" table maps directly onto the paper's own vocabulary: story trajectory, segments (Donné, Disturbance, Plan/Transit, Enact, Celebrate), coherence, and "reverse engineering" (paper's coda, p. 19–21)
  - Sidenote frames Benzon's black-box probing as analogous to the paper's own invocation of Pinker's reverse-engineering definition and the Anthropic induction-heads example (p. 19–20)
- Three-level architecture
  - Paper explicitly proposes surface / middle / bottom levels (p. 19–20) for describing ChatGPT's behavior
  - Sidenote's "signal processing view" (whole story \u2192 segments \u2192 sentences \u2192 tokens) and "nested hierarchy of probability distributions" slide directly restate this three/four-level structure as Benzon's "main hypothesis"
- Reverse engineering discussion
  - Paper's coda traces reverse engineering from Broadbent/Pinker through Anthropic's mechanistic interpretability work (p. 19)
  - Sidenote reframes this as "black-box behavioural probing via systematic perturbation" and positions Benzon alongside Haralick & Ramesh's performance-characterisation framework, extending the paper's own comparison to interpretability research
- Competence vs. performance
  - Paper quotes David Hays on Chomsky's competence/performance distinction (p. 20) to argue ChatGPT's sentence-level output is "performance," implemented in the middle-level weights
  - Sidenote does not directly cite Hays/Chomsky but implicitly builds on this framing when treating segment/sentence output as the observable "performance" layer probed via perturbation
- Extension beyond the paper's scope
  - Sidenote's synthetic Markov-sequence / bit-flip noise experiments (Transformer vs. k-gram) are the student's own project, not in Benzon's paper, but are explicitly presented as a quantitative analogue to Benzon's qualitative character-substitution perturbations
  - Sidenote's proposed "how to make Benzon's approach more rigorous" section (multiple stories per condition, controlled parameters, embeddings) is the student's critique/extension, using Haralick & Ramesh as the rigor benchmark the paper's own coda gestures toward but does not formalize
- Citations reused from the paper
  - Sidenote's references slide reproduces the paper's own citation (Benzon 2023, "ChatGPT tells stories, and a note about reverse engineering") plus the companion 20-versions paper referenced within it (p. 20–21 discussion of story sampling), and adds the Haralick/Ramesh vision-science literature as an external framework not present in the paper itself
